text: A conurbation is a big urban area formed when neighbouring towns and cities grow until they join together. Here it means Europe's major city areas, which grew until they fit their own countries.
Middling means medium or average, neither great nor terrible. The article uses it for cities that are mid-sized: Europe has many of them but no giant.
Sprawl is the uncontrolled spread of a city outward into open land. European cities sometimes grew past their old medieval edges even though planning laws tried to stop it.
A metropolis is a very large, important city, usually the main economic centre of a region. Here the writer asks whether Europe's cities can match the advantages of true metropolises like New York.
A standard-bearer was the soldier who carried the flag in battle. Now it means the leading example of a group, here Paris as the biggest city of the European Union.
Underwhelming is the opposite of overwhelming: it means disappointing or less impressive than expected. Paris looks small next to Shanghai and New York.
A flagship was the main ship of a fleet. Today it means the best or most important example of something, such as a company's top product or, here, a union's leading city.
Ville Lumière is French for City of Light, a nickname for Paris. It reflects the city's early streetlights and its role in the Age of Enlightenment.
Dauntingly means in a way that makes you feel nervous or overwhelmed. To a tourist with only a few days, Paris can seem too large to see.
Smothering literally means blocking someone's air, and figuratively means controlling or overwhelming in a suffocating way. The French sometimes feel Paris's power over the country is smothering.
Bloated means swollen, too big for its purpose. Here it describes Paris as an administrative headquarters that has grown oversized.
Over-centralised means too much power and activity sit in one place. France is the classic case, with most government and business decisions made in Paris.
The EU, or European Union, is a group of 27 European countries that share a single market, many laws and, for many members, one currency.
Urbanised means that most people live in cities and towns rather than the countryside. Europe is a largely urbanised continent.
Dynamism is energy and constant change, especially in an economy full of new businesses and ideas. The article argues Europe needs more of it.

The Economist Intelligence Unit is the research and analysis arm of The Economist's parent group, which is why the article calls it a sister company. Its yearly liveability ranking scores cities on things like safety, health care and culture.
Heft means weight, and commercial heft means real economic weight and influence. The article says Europe's charming cities often lack it.
A hinterland is the land behind a coast or a city, usually rural. China and India have vast rural hinterlands, yet their biggest cities still produce a larger share of national output.
Economic output is the total value of the goods and services an area produces. It is the main way the article compares cities.
Et alors? is French for So what? The writer imagines a sceptic who asks why Europe needs bigger cities at all.

This is a joke place name: sur-Seine means on the Seine, the river through Paris. The writer imagines Paris becoming as huge as Jakarta. Tokyo am Rhein, a Tokyo on the Rhine, plays the same trick in German.
To cram is to squeeze many things into a small space. The economists' idea is that packing more people close together makes the city richer.
Productivity is how much output a worker or firm produces in an hour or with a given set of resources. Higher productivity is the main source of rising living standards.
The OECD, the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development, is a club of mostly rich countries that collects data and gives advice on economic policy.
Congestion means overcrowding, especially traffic jams and packed public transport. It is a cost of big cities.
Amenities are features that make a place pleasant to live in, such as parks, theatres and sports stadiums. The article says they help make up for crowds and high rents.
To seep is to flow slowly through a small gap, like water through soil. The article uses it for cities gradually leaking out past their medieval walls.
Medieval refers to the Middle Ages, roughly the years 500 to 1500. Many European cities began then, with tight boundaries.
A polity is an organised political community such as a country or region. The article means that no European city is likely to drift away from the nation it belongs to.
European integration means the process by which European countries joined their economies and laws through the EU. In theory it should make the whole EU feel like one home market.
A megalopolis is a huge region of connected cities, even larger than a metropolis. The article says integration should have created a handful of these.
Oomph is informal for power, energy or impact. No European city has the oomph of New York in finance.
Up to snuff is an idiom meaning meeting the required standard. Here the writer says Europe's mid-sized capitals are not quite good enough to compete globally, with a quick sorry to Prague.
A winner-takes-most market is one where the top few firms or places capture most of the rewards. AI is the article's example, which is why scattered European hubs struggle.
Silicon Valley is the area around San Francisco that is home to many of the world's biggest technology companies and start-ups.
To gnaw is to bite at something steadily, wearing it down. Here it means that the spread-out nature of Europe's cities slowly harms its competitiveness.
To console yourself means to find comfort after a disappointment. The article offers two comforting thoughts to Europeans.
A hub is a central point where lots of activity meets, and a mega-hub is a very large one. The question is whether linked cities could act as one.
To decay means to gradually weaken. The benefits of sharing a place shrink fast as distance grows, even across short train rides.
Feeling left behind means believing that the economy and politicians have ignored your community while others, usually in big cities, prosper.
Flyover country is an American phrase for the middle of the country that people on the coasts only see from a plane window. It is used mockingly by some urban elites.
To sneer is to show contempt with a mocking tone or expression. Europe, the writer says, lacks a big gap between sneering elites and the places they look down on.
Wee is Scottish and informal for very small. It adds a gentle humour to the article's closing description of Europe's many small cities.
